summary: For ages 8-9: find 1000 more or less than a four-digit number by recognising that normally only the thousands digit changes (4,562 → 5,562 or 3,562), extending the earlier +10/+100 pattern into the next place. The key exceptions are boundary crossings: adding 1000 when the thousands digit is 9 regroups into the ten-thousands place (9,500 + 1000 = 10,500), and subtracting 1000 can remove or reduce a higher digit (1,562 − 1000 = 562; 10,500 − 1000 = 9,500). Learners should justify which digit changes, not count on in smaller steps, and generalise beyond 10,000, where crossings such as 19,500 + 1000 = 20,500 change the ten-thousands digit too.
misconceptions: Changing the wrong digit (stepping hundreds instead of thousands).
Counting on in smaller steps instead of jumping the place.
Assuming only one digit ever changes, mishandling roll-over.

activities.title: Digit-stepper: which column responds to +1000?
steps: Start from a four-digit number such as 4,562 shown in a place-value chart or on a number line.
Press +1000 (and −1000) and observe which digit moves: the thousands digit ticks 4→5 for +1000 (giving 5,562) or 4→3 for −1000 (giving 3,562) while hundreds, tens and ones stay locked.
Before each press, predict the result and name the digit that will change; then check against what moves.
Compare +10, +100 and +1000 side by side on the same starting number, saying which column each operation drives.
Use a 0–10,000 number-line view to see ±1000 as equal hops along the line.
activities.insight: Adding or subtracting 1000 normally changes only the thousands digit, extending the same place-value logic that governs +10 and +100.

activities.title: The roll-over: when a place fills up
steps: Start from a boundary number such as 9,500 or 9,300.
Press +1000 and watch the thousands digit pass 9: it rolls 9→0 while a carry moves left, opening a new ten-thousands column (9,500 → 10,500; 9,300 → 10,300).
State in words why the number gains a digit: 9 thousands + 1 thousand = 10 thousands.
Rehearse just the single roll in reasoning: 9 thousands + 1 thousand = 10 thousands, so 9,300 + 1000 = 10,300 — not 0,300, not 9,300, not 19,300.
Try numbers beyond 10,000 to confirm the same place-value rule continues, including crossings such as 19,500 + 1000 = 20,500 and 10,500 − 1000 = 9,500.
activities.insight: When the thousands digit passes 9, the 'only one digit changes' pattern has a principled exception: the place fills up and regroups into the ten-thousands place (opening a new place for 9,500 → 10,500, or raising an existing ten-thousands digit for 19,500 → 20,500); the reverse crossing happens when subtracting (10,500 − 1000 = 9,500).

activities.title: Scored fluency and boundary checks
steps: Answer fill-in items such as '1000 more than 4,562 = __' and '1000 less than 4,562 = __'.
Answer which-digit-changes questions for ordinary cases.
Tackle boundary items deliberately, e.g. 9,500 + 1000 and 9,300 + 1000, writing the full regrouped answer.
Use a slider on a 0–10,000 line to land exactly 1000 away from a given point.
activities.insight: Secure, quick retrieval of 1000 more/less, including the regrouping boundary, confirms the place-value reasoning is fluent.

checkQuestion: Ask quickly and watch the method: '1000 more than 4,562? ... 1000 less than 4,562? ... 1000 more than 9,300?' The last one crosses into the ten-thousands — watch what happens.
checkAnswer: 5,562; 3,562; 10,300 — changing only the thousands digit, and rolling into a new place when it passes 9.
